office: I should probably focus. Right after this dramatic pause.
This office smells like dust, secrets, and coffee that lost its will to live.
An agent's greatest weapon is observation. The second greatest is a receipt for expenses.
I should look busy. In this business, looking busy is half the investigation.
Somewhere out there, a criminal is making a mistake. Ideally one involving paperwork.
The agency calls it an open-door policy. Most of the doors are locked.
I joined a detective agency. Naturally, everyone has something to hide.
Somebody straightened the picture again. There are limits to what I will investigate.
The clock is loud for someone contributing so little.
I can recognise six kinds of forged signature. Still cannot identify my lunch in the fridge.
A good question saves hours. A bad question gets you invited to a meeting.
This building has excellent acoustics. Everyone hears the gossip. Nobody hears their name being called.
There is a difference between a theory and a hunch. Usually about three witnesses.
Every department says the problem belongs to another department. An unusually well-coordinated alibi.
I should stretch my legs. They have been supporting this investigation from the beginning.
The office plant is leaning towards the exit. Observant little thing.
lab: Nothing says justice like fluorescent lighting.
If this machine explodes, I am blaming science.
hotel: A hotel room: temporary headquarters, permanent source of suspicious carpet patterns.
I should sleep. The case will still be confusing in the morning.
The minibar is staring at me like it knows I cannot expense this.
Some detectives chase leads. I am currently chasing eight uninterrupted hours of sleep.
New city, new room, same problem: criminals refuse to work office hours.
The wallpaper has seen things. None of them are admissible in court.
I could review the evidence. Or I could lie down and call it strategic thinking.
A good detective follows the clues. A tired detective follows the smell of hotel coffee.

lockedDrawer: Locked. Which is rude, but informative.
desk: A desk. The natural habitat of unpaid invoices.
Nothing suspicious here. Which is, frankly, suspicious.
Three drawers. All of them judging me.
The desk is clean. That is either professionalism or an alibi.
A place to assemble a warrant. Preferably before assembling an apology.
The blotter has absorbed decades of ink. It knows better than to talk.
The pen is chained to the desk. Finally, some effective crime prevention.
I should check the details before signing. My signature is not a substitute for evidence.
globe: A globe. Proof that trouble can be geographically ambitious.
So many cities. So little budget for taxis.
Spin the globe, pick a city, ruin a criminal's afternoon.
No borders on the oceans. Criminals find that encouraging.
The whole world, balanced on a small metal pin. I understand the feeling.
From this distance, every getaway looks poorly planned.
The globe rotates freely. International cooperation is a little stiffer.
A useful reminder: a flight ticket is not an alibi.
fakePainting: A fake. And not even an ambitious one.
ledger: All these columns, and not one offers emotional support.
The accounts should balance. Unlike most witness statements.
A receipt is just evidence with a tax number.
Financial irregularities. Finally, suspects that stay on the page.
Every expense needs a category. Apparently, "it seemed sensible at the time" is not one.
The ledger records what we spent. It politely omits what we were thinking.
Numbers do not lie. They do, however, require unusually close supervision.
crimeBoard: The crime board: string, pins, and the fragile illusion that I know what I am doing.
Every clue has a place. Usually directly under another clue I forgot to read.
The board is ready. Now I only need facts, motive, opportunity, and several miracles.
A connecting thread proves a connection between two pins. The rest still needs evidence.
The neatest theory is not necessarily the right one. Annoying, but important.
If every suspect fits, I have probably described a person rather than a criminal.
A good timeline is hard to argue with. People still try.
I need to separate what happened from what would make an excellent ending.
caseFileCabinet: Case files: the place where every mystery begins with too much paperwork.
Some detectives trust instinct. I trust folders labelled 'URGENT'.
A filing cabinet. The natural predator of forgotten leads.
Filed alphabetically. Except for the things filed emotionally.
The important details rarely announce themselves. They hide halfway down page seven.
A folder can look innocent and still contain an entire afternoon.
Official records. Where a missing comma can acquire a supervisor.
Best read the brief before developing a strongly held opinion about it.
notesBook: My notes. Written in a code known only to me and future forensic linguists.
If I cannot read my own handwriting, neither can the criminals.
A good detective keeps notes. A great detective remembers where they put them.
A question mark is not evidence. I have underlined this several times.
Past me wrote "obvious" and provided no further assistance.
The margins contain my best ideas and an increasingly elaborate duck.
Write down the exact words. Memory enjoys a little creative editing.
No loose pages. A gust of wind should not be able to solve the case before I do.
wantedDatabase: Wanted suspects. Mostly terrible people with surprisingly good cheekbones.
A database full of faces. One of them is probably about to make my day worse.
Criminal records: social media, but with more warrants.
An alias is useful. Remembering which alias you gave the police is apparently harder.
The photograph identifies a face. It does not explain what that face was doing on Tuesday.
Some of these disguises rely heavily on people being polite.
One distinguishing feature is not an identification. Even if it is an extraordinary moustache.
A criminal record is a lead, not permission to skip the investigation.
recoveredArtifacts: Recovered artefacts. History has a habit of getting stolen by people with poor taste.
Every artefact has survived centuries. Then someone tried to sell it online.
A shelf of treasures, each with a story and an insurance claim.
Museums call it provenance. I call it finding out whose attic it passed through.
Centuries of craftsmanship. Defeated by someone carrying a sports bag.
Please do not touch. Good advice for visitors, burglars, and curious detectives.
Authenticity matters. A dramatic backstory is not a certificate.
The oldest things in this building are not necessarily the most out of date.
atlas: An atlas. Because criminals insist on fleeing somewhere picturesque.
Maps never show the queues, the jet lag, or the suspiciously expensive airport sandwiches.
The world is large. Fortunately, criminals are fond of leaving clues.
An index. For when my extensive geographical knowledge needs alphabetical assistance.
Distance is straightforward. Connections are where the trouble starts.
A place name can be a clue. It can also be a restaurant. Context matters.
Tiny print, enormous countries. A bold editorial decision.
The map is not out of date. The world has been making unauthorised changes.
brokenElevator: Out of order. A bold career choice for an elevator.
The elevator is dead. It had a good run. Mostly between floors.
A sign says 'Out of Order.' At least someone here is being honest.
The button lights up. A convincing performance, but no actual movement.
The doors are closed. The investigation into why they remain closed is ongoing.
A machine with one job and a firm commitment to boundaries.
I pressed once. Pressing twelve more times would be interrogation, not maintenance.
The floor indicator has chosen a floor and intends to defend its position.
hotelBed: A hotel bed. It has seen worse decisions than sleeping before checking the clues.
The mattress is lumpy, but the detective is tired enough to call it character.
Sleep now, solve crimes later. That is not procrastination. It is field recovery.
The pillow has the emotional support rating of a folded receipt.
hotelTv: Local news is on. Somewhere, a reporter is using the phrase 'shocking development'.
The television knows more about the city than I do. Rude, but useful.
Breaking news: crime continues to exist. Experts remain unsurprised.
The anchor looks concerned. Either there is a crime wave or the teleprompter broke.
hotelDesk: A hotel desk: small, wobbly, and still somehow better organised than my office.
The desk is perfect for reviewing clues, writing notes, and hiding the minibar bill.
Evidence, string, pins, and room service receipts. A proper mobile headquarters.
A crime board in a hotel room is either dedication or a very specific kind of problem.
hotelWindow: The city is out there. Somewhere in it, a criminal is ruining my schedule.
A beautiful view. Statistically, at least three people outside are lying.
The streets are calling. Unfortunately, they are also charging taxi fares.
Time to leave the room before the wallpaper starts offering legal advice.

noMission: No active assignment. A rare opportunity to read the instructions before ignoring them.
I should check the agency computer for a case. Staring meaningfully at the door has produced nothing.
No case on my desk. Best enjoy the visible wood while it lasts.
I can organise my notes now, or rediscover this opportunity halfway through a crisis.
Between assignments. The only time "nothing to report" sounds promising.
missionAccepted: New assignment. First, establish what is missing. Then establish who is exaggerating.
I should read the brief before booking anything. Geography is less forgiving than enthusiasm.
The case is open. My conclusions can remain closed until I have some evidence.
An artefact, a theft, and an official account of events. One of those may need correcting.
Time to get the facts in order. They rarely arrive that way.
missionSuccess: One case closed. I should write the report while the facts still outnumber the anecdotes.
The result held up. Always satisfying when the evidence survives meeting other people.
Back at the agency with a successful case. I shall try not to walk past the same colleagues twice.
For the record, that was deduction. Any sweating was incidental.
A good result. Now comes the difficult part: explaining it without moving my hands.
missionFailure: That did not work. The useful question is where it stopped working.
I need to review the case, not rewrite it with a more flattering ending.
The next investigation needs better checks, not a more confident expression.
A bad result is not a mystery. There will be a point where I missed something.
Back to the evidence. It deserves another look, even if my pride would prefer a transfer.
ledgerLowBudget: The remaining budget is beginning to look like a rounding error.
I should plan the next expense carefully. The ledger has stopped finding me charming.
These figures suggest a strategy best described as "nearby".
Not much room for unnecessary spending. I should establish what is necessary before the airport does.
The available funds could use a witness protection programme. There are very few of them left.
Before I authorise another expense, I should check whether the decimal point is where I hoped.
ledgerHealthyBudget: There is room in the budget. That is not the same as an invitation.
The funds are available. Accounting will still want to know why.
A workable budget. I can investigate the crime instead of the price of a sandwich.
The accounts leave us some options. Best choose one that also produces evidence.
Enough funding to proceed sensibly. I shall resist the urge to celebrate on expenses.
